title: Relative dynamic subgroups of a smooth affine group
statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $X=\operatorname{Spec}R$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], and $G$ a smooth affine $R$-group scheme of finite presentation [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation]. Group schemes over $X$ have multiplication, inverse and identity satisfying the group diagrams over $X$. Let $a:\mathbf G_{m,R}\times_R G\to G$ be an action by group automorphisms, where $\mathbf G_{m,R}=\operatorname{Spec}R[t,t^{-1}]$. Write $-a$ for $a(t^{-1},g)$. For a commutative $R$-algebra $B$, define $P_a(B)$ by requiring the orbit $t\mapsto a(t,g)$ to extend to $\mathbf A^1_B\to G_B$, define $U_a(B)$ by requiring also that its value at $0$ is $1$, and define $Z_a(B)$ by requiring $a(t,g)=g$ after every $B$-algebra extension and for every unit $t$. These functors are represented by smooth affine finitely presented closed subgroup schemes of $G$ [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Evaluation at zero is a homomorphism $q:P_a\to Z_a$ with kernel $U_a$; $U_a$ is normal in $P_a$, and multiplication is an isomorphism $Z_a\ltimes U_a\simeq P_a$, whose underlying scheme map is $(z,u)\mapsto zu$ and whose group law is induced by conjugation. The multiplication map $U_{-a}\times_R P_a\to G$ is an open immersion [def-weil-open-immersion]. The geometric fibres of $U_a$ are connected and unipotent (their geometric points are unipotent matrices in a faithful representation); if $G$ has geometrically connected fibres, so do $P_a$ and $Z_a$ [def-weil-connected-scheme].
Writing $\mathfrak g=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf Z}\mathfrak g_n$ for the integer-character weight decomposition of the tangent module at the identity under $a$, their tangent submodules are $\operatorname{Lie}(Z_a)=\mathfrak g_0$, $\operatorname{Lie}(U_a)=\bigoplus_{n>0}\mathfrak g_n$ and $\operatorname{Lie}(P_a)=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}\mathfrak g_n$. Tangents here are dual-number points reducing to the identity. All these subgroup schemes, inclusions, maps and tangent identifications commute with arbitrary and successive base change $R\to R'$. Explicitly, if $C=R[G]=\bigoplus C_n$ with $f(a(t,g))=t^nf(g)$ for $f\in C_n$ and with identity evaluation $\epsilon:C\to R$, then $P_a$ is cut out by the ideal generated by $C_n$ for $n<0$, $Z_a$ by all $C_n$ for $n\ne0$, and $U_a$ by the negative-degree elements together with $f-\epsilon(f)$ for $f\in C_0$.

source.place: Conrad, Reductive group schemes, Theorem 4.1.7(1)-(4), printed pp.112-114; the paragraph after Example 4.1.9, p.114 (arbitrary base change). The proof specifies the coordinate ideals on p.113. No reductivity or root system is assumed.

proof.text:
Put $C=R[G]$. The action coaction and [lem-sfb-group-algebra-coaction-grading], with character group $\mathbf Z$, give the grading in the statement. Since the identity is fixed, $\epsilon(C_n)=0$ for $n
e0$, by comparing Laurent coefficients. A point $g:C	o B$ has orbit homomorphism $f_n\mapsto g(f_n)t^n$. It lands in $B[t]\subset B[t,t^{-1}]$ exactly when $g(C_n)=0$ for $n<0$. Uniqueness follows from injectivity of this polynomial inclusion over every ring. Thus $C/(C_{<0})$ represents $P_a$. Comparing Laurent coefficients in the universal unit $t$ shows that a point is fixed after all algebra extensions exactly when $g(C_n)=0$ for $n
e0$. Hence $C/(C_{
e0})$ represents $Z_a$. Multiplication and inverse of orbit extensions are again orbit extensions, so these are closed subgroup schemes on every test algebra.

source.place: Theorem 4.1.7, proof, printed pp.113-114; agent supplies the coordinate and infinitesimal details.

proof.text: Write $A=C/(C_{<0})$, a nonnegatively graded algebra. Its degree-zero projection defines a homomorphism $q:P_a\to Z_a$: if $p(t)$ is the orbit extension, then $a(s,p(t))=p(st)$, and setting $t=0$ proves that $p(0)$ is fixed. The identities $q(gh)=q(g)q(h)$ and $q(z)=z$ follow by evaluating products and constant orbits. Its fibre over $1$ has coordinate ideal generated by the negative-degree elements and $f-\epsilon(f)$ for $f\in C_0$, giving exactly the stated $U_a$. To check finite presentation, choose finitely many homogeneous algebra generators $x_i$ for $C$ by taking all components of any finite generating set. The negative ideal is generated by the $x_i$ of negative degree, since every negative-weight monomial contains one. Modulo it, the positive ideal is generated by the positive-degree $x_i$, and the degree-zero algebra is generated by the zero-degree $x_i$. Consequently the fixed ideal is generated by all nonzero-degree $x_i$, and the kernel ideal by the negative $x_i$ and $x_i-\epsilon(x_i)$ of degree zero. All three are finitely generated ideals in a finitely presented algebra, so all three quotient algebras are finitely presented over $R$.

source.place: Theorem 4.1.7, proof, printed pp.113-114; agent supplies the coordinate and infinitesimal details.

proof.text: The kernel calculation makes $U_a$ normal in $P_a$. Conjugation by $Z_a$ preserves it. For every algebra $B$, the maps $(z,u)\mapsto zu$ and $g\mapsto(q(g),q(g)^{-1}g)$ are mutually inverse and natural, since $q$ is a retraction and a homomorphism. They are scheme morphisms built from $q$, multiplication and inverse. Transporting multiplication gives $(z,u)(z',u')=(zz',(z')^{-1}uz'\,u')$. This proves the asserted semidirect-product isomorphism with the specified order $zu$; no assertion about sets of geometric points alone is used.

source.place: Theorem 4.1.7, proof, printed pp.113-114; agent supplies the coordinate and infinitesimal details.

proof.text: For a square-zero ideal $I\subset B$ and a point of $P_a(B/I)$, its orbit gives a graded homomorphism $C\to(B/I)[t]$, with $\deg t=1$ and $B/I$ in degree zero. Apply [lem-sfb-graded-square-zero-smooth-lifting] to $D=B[t]$ and the homogeneous square-zero ideal $I[t]$. The graded lift, evaluated at $t=1$, is a lift to $P_a(B)$, because it kills all negative-degree components. For a point of $Z_a(B/I)$ use instead $D=B$ concentrated in degree zero; the graded lift kills every $C_n$ for $n\ne0$ and so lies in $Z_a(B)$. Thus both affine schemes have the square-zero lifting property. By [lem-weil-pbc-affine-formally-smooth-iff-ring-lifting] they are formally smooth, and their finite presentation from step 2 makes them smooth by [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms].

source.place: Theorem 4.1.7, proof, printed pp.113-114; agent supplies the coordinate and infinitesimal details.

proof.text: To lift $u_0\in U_a(B/I)$ across $I^2=0$, first lift it to $p\in P_a(B)$ by step 4. Put $z=q(p)$. Since $q(u_0)=1$, $z$ reduces to $1$, and $z^{-1}p$ reduces to $u_0$ and lies in the kernel of $q$. Thus $U_a$ has the square-zero lifting property. Its finite presentation from step 2 and [lem-weil-pbc-affine-formally-smooth-iff-ring-lifting, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] imply smoothness. Apply steps 1-5 with the action $-a$ as well: it satisfies the same hypotheses, so in particular $U_{-a}$ is smooth affine finitely presented.

source.place: Theorem 4.1.7, proof, printed pp.113-114; agent supplies the coordinate and infinitesimal details.

proof.text: The coordinate algebra $D=R[U_a]$ is nonnegatively graded with $D_0=R$: the degree-zero quotient sends every $f\in C_0$ to $\epsilon(f)$, and the identity section splits $R\to D$. The homomorphism $D\to D[s]$, $f_n\mapsto s^nf_n$, defines a contraction $\mathbf A^1_R\times_R U_a\to U_a$, equal to the identity at $s=1$ and the constant identity section at $s=0$. After any algebraically closed base field $F$, every point $x$ of $U_{a,F}$ gives a morphism $\mathbf A^1_{\kappa(x)}\to U_{a,F}$ by applying this contraction to its canonical $\kappa(x)$-point. Its image contains $x$ and the identity point. The source is irreducible, since the zero prime of the domain $\kappa(x)[s]$ is generic; its image is connected. Hence every point belongs to the identity's connected component, proving connectedness of the entire geometric fibre, including nonclosed points.

source.place: Theorem 4.1.7, proof, printed pp.113-114; agent supplies the coordinate and infinitesimal details.

proof.text: For an algebraically closed $R$-field $F$, form the affine finite-type $F$-scheme $J=G_F\times_F\mathbf G_{m,F}$. Define $(g,s)(h,t)=(g\,a(s,h),st)$, inverse $(g,s)^{-1}=(a(s^{-1},g^{-1}),s^{-1})$, and identity $(1,1)$. The action and group identities verify associativity and both inverse identities directly, so these morphisms make $J$ an affine finite-type group scheme. The maps $i(g)=(g,1)$ and $\lambda(t)=(1,t)$ are homomorphisms and $\lambda(t)i(g)\lambda(t)^{-1}=i(a(t,g))$. The map $i$ is a closed immersion: on $F[J]=F[G_F][z,z^{-1}]$ it is the quotient $z\mapsto1$. This construction is only over the field $F$, and requires no linear embedding theorem over $R$.

source.place: Theorem 4.1.7, proof, printed pp.113-114; agent supplies the coordinate and infinitesimal details.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-affine-group-faithful-linear-representation] to $J$ of step 7 to get a closed immersion $\rho:J\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}_{m,F}$. Its restriction along $i$ is closed, since both coordinate homomorphisms are surjective. By [lem-sfb-gm-representation-weight-basis], choose a basis for $\rho\lambda$ with integer weights $d_1\geq\cdots\geq d_m$. For $u\in U_a(F)$, let $M=\rho i(u)$. Conjugation in step 7 shows that the $(i,j)$ entry along its orbit is $t^{d_i-d_j}M_{ij}$. The orbit extends to $\mathbf A^1_F$ with value the identity at zero, and composing it with $\rho i$ gives polynomial matrix entries. Comparing Laurent coefficients gives $M_{ij}=0$ when $d_i<d_j$, $M_{ij}=0$ when $d_i=d_j$ and $i\ne j$, and $M_{ii}=1$. Thus $M-I$ is strictly upper triangular, and every product of $m$ of its entries along increasing indices is zero; hence $(M-I)^m=0$. This proves unipotence in a faithful representation on each geometric fibre. The same argument with $-a$ applies to $U_{-a}$.

source.place: Theorem 4.9 and Corollary 4.10, printed p.87; Theorem 12.12 and Remark 12.13, printed pp.234-235. Agent applies these to the explicitly constructed semidirect product over each geometric field and computes its contracting matrices.

proof.text: A tangent vector at $1$ over an $R$-module $M$ is a homomorphism to the square-zero algebra $R\oplus M$ of the form $f\mapsto\epsilon(f)+\delta(f)$; multiplicativity says precisely that $\delta(fg)=\epsilon(f)\delta(g)+\epsilon(g)\delta(f)$ and $\delta(R)=0$. The universal property in [def-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials] identifies these with $\operatorname{Hom}_R(E,M)$, $E=\Omega_{C/R}\otimes_{C,\epsilon}R$. On a homogeneous $f_m$, the action sends $\delta(f_m)$ to $t^m\delta(f_m)$. Splitting a derivation into its restrictions to the homogeneous components preserves the displayed Leibniz identity, since $\epsilon$ kills nonzero weights. These are exactly its weight components, with finite support because a derivation is determined by its values on the finite homogeneous generators from step 2. The ideals of steps 1-2 then impose, respectively, vanishing of the negative components, of all nonzero components, and of the nonpositive components. This gives $\operatorname{Lie}(P_a)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\mathfrak g_n$, $\operatorname{Lie}(Z_a)=\mathfrak g_0$, and $\operatorname{Lie}(U_a)=\bigoplus_{n>0}\mathfrak g_n$, with their actual inclusions into the tangent module of $G$.

source.place: Theorem 4.1.7, proof, printed pp.113-114; agent supplies the coordinate and infinitesimal details.

proof.text: For every algebra $B$, a point of $U_{-a}\cap P_a$ kills the positive and negative homogeneous components of $C$, and on degree zero has value $\epsilon$. It is therefore the identity, so the intersection is the trivial subgroup functor. Over every algebraically closed $R$-field $F$, the tangent formulas of step 9 give complementary subspaces $\operatorname{Lie}(U_{-a,F})=\mathfrak g_{F,<0}$ and $\operatorname{Lie}(P_{a,F})=\mathfrak g_{F,\ge0}$ inside $\operatorname{Lie}(G_F)$. Here the coordinate formulas also identify the base-changed functors directly. Apply [lem-sfb-transverse-subgroup-product-open] to these smooth closed subgroups over $F$: multiplication is an open immersion on that fibre. All three group schemes are affine finitely presented over $R$. The multiplication map is finitely presented: choose finite presentations of its source and target algebras over $R$ and add finitely many relations specifying the images of the target generators. Its source is smooth, since tensor products of smooth affine algebras are smooth by the base-change and composition clauses of [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-ring-map-base-change-composition] and [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-ring-map-iff-smooth-affine]. Therefore [lem-sfb-flat-geometric-fibre-open-criterion] applies and makes $U_{-a}\times_RP_a\to G$ an open immersion over $R$.

source.place: Theorem 4.1.7, proof, printed pp.113-114; agent supplies the coordinate and infinitesimal details.

proof.text: Suppose now that the geometric fibres of $G$ are connected, and fix an algebraically closed $R$-field $F$. By [lem-sfb-locally-algebraic-group-identity-component], the connected finite-type group $G_F$ equals its identity component and is irreducible. The nonempty open image $W$ of step 10 is consequently irreducible and hence connected. Via the open immersion it is isomorphic to $U_{-a,F}\times_FP_{a,F}$. Projection onto $P_{a,F}$ is surjective, since the identity of the first factor is a section. Its image is therefore connected. The retraction $q_F$ is also surjective (with section $Z_{a,F}\hookrightarrow P_{a,F}$), so $Z_{a,F}$ is connected. This proves geometric connectedness of both groups; it does not assume connectedness of them in order to apply the open-cell argument.

source.place: Theorem 4.1.7, proof, printed pp.113-114; agent supplies the coordinate and infinitesimal details.

proof.text: For any $R\to R'$, tensor the direct-sum grading of $C$ with $R'$. The ideals defining the three groups become exactly the ideals generated by the corresponding homogeneous components of $R'\otimes_RC$ (tensor preserves quotients and direct sums). Their generators for $U$ use the scalar-extended identity evaluation. Thus all subgroup inclusions are the stated arbitrary base changes. The formulas for $q$, multiplication, conjugation, and the semidirect inverse use only identity evaluation and the group maps, so their base changes are the same formulas. For tangents, [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-ring-map-iff-smooth-affine] and [def-weil-pbc-smooth-ring-map] make $\Omega_{C/R}$ finite projective; its pullback $E$ along $\epsilon$ is therefore a summand of some $R^N$. By [lem-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials-base-change], the new identity cotangent module is $R'\otimes_RE$. The natural map $R'\otimes_RE^*\to(R'\otimes_RE)^*$ sends $b\otimes\phi$ to $(c\otimes v\mapsto bc\phi(v))$; it is an isomorphism for $E=R^N$ by coordinates and hence on its specified direct summand. This proves tangent base change. It preserves the weight projections computed in step 9, since their defining Laurent coefficient maps tensor to those over $R'$. All comparisons commute with a further $R'\to R''$: on ring elements, quotient generators and elementary tensors both composites are the identical formulas. This includes the zero ring, empty base, trivial action (giving $P=Z=G,U=1$), and the trivial group.
